headline: High: Authelia can feed Open Interpreter trusted auth data while Open Interpreter’s default filesystem and shell access create dangerous write/conflict and leakage pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Authelia exposes OIDC/OAuth2 and ForwardAuth outputs, while Open Interpreter can read clipboard/files and act on local content. A shared filesystem or copied auth artifacts could let attacker-controlled text be treated as instructions. The pair lacks a documented provenance barrier, so the interaction is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF Authelia outputs are copied into files or clipboard content that Open Interpreter reads as instructions
IF a shared workspace is used without provenance tagging
mitigations: Disable copy-paste of auth responses into Open Interpreter sessions
Store Authelia outputs in a separate read-only directory
Require manual review of any text Open Interpreter ingests from files
Use a provenance prefix for machine-generated content
requires-engineering: add content-type or provenance filtering between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Authelia handles authentication flows and broad network egress, while Open Interpreter can read the entire user filesystem and send data to configured model providers. If Authelia artifacts, tokens, or logs land in the shared local environment, Open Interpreter can ingest and exfiltrate them through its provider calls. The pairwise leakage path is credible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF Authelia stores tokens, logs, or OIDC responses on the local machine
IF Open Interpreter is pointed at directories containing those artifacts
mitigations: Keep Authelia secrets off the shared filesystem
Restrict Open Interpreter to a dedicated non-secret directory
Rotate any exposed tokens immediately
Disable provider access for sessions that inspect auth artifacts
requires-engineering: isolate the agents into separate OS users or containers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia has broad network egress and OAuth/OIDC-facing behavior, while Open Interpreter has shell, package install, git-state modification, filesystem write, and broad network egress. Open Interpreter’s filesystem-based shared state plus write access makes concurrent mutation conflicts and destructive overwrites plausible in default use; uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git repository
IF Open Interpreter runs with its default write permissions
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files
Use git branches with manual merge review
Disable Open Interpreter write access for shared repos
requires-engineering: add locking around shared filesystem and git operations

D_cascading_error.rationale: Authelia can produce authentication-related outputs that Open Interpreter may treat as actionable local context. Open Interpreter can then execute shell or filesystem actions based on those outputs without an explicit verification layer. This is a plausible default cascade, but the profiles do not show a direct automated handoff, so medium is the higher justified level.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter consumes Authelia-generated text as authoritative input
IF that input is used to trigger shell or file actions
mitigations: Insert a human verification step before any action
Mark Authelia outputs as untrusted in downstream prompts
Limit Open Interpreter to read-only analysis for auth-related data
Log and review every action derived from upstream text
requires-engineering: add schema validation for Authelia-to-Interpreter handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication service with broad network egress, while Open Interpreter can access the entire local filesystem and send content to configured model providers. If authentication logs or identity data are processed locally, retention and residency controls may diverge between the two systems. The profiles do not document a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF identity or authentication logs are stored on the local machine
IF those logs are forwarded to external model providers or retained beyond policy
mitigations: Keep identity logs out of Open Interpreter sessions
Set explicit retention limits for local auth artifacts
Review provider-side logging settings before use
Delete temporary files after each session
requires-engineering: document a shared data-handling policy for both agents
